title: Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk: The Birth of a Democratic South Africa — 1991
summary: During the 1991 CODESA negotiations in Johannesburg, Nelson Mandela boldly confronted President F. W. de Klerk, demanding genuine majority democracy over cosmetic compromises.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 143: காந்தியும் செய்தியாளர்களும்: “ப்ளஸ்-ஃபோர்ஸ் வேண்டாம்; மைனஸ்-ஃபோர்ஸ்!”
full_text:
In December 1991, inside the World Trade Centre near Johannesburg, South Africa embarked upon the Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA) to negotiate an end to apartheid.

Nelson Mandela, released after twenty-seven years of imprisonment, sat opposite President F. W. de Klerk. Taking the podium at the end of the day's session, De Klerk launched an unexpected attack on the African National Congress, seeking to retain minority vetoes and protect apartheid-era privileges.

Mandela’s face set like granite. Deviating from standard diplomatic protocol, he walked back to the microphone, his voice cutting through the hall with thunderous clarity:
"Mr. de Klerk, even the head of an illegitimate, discredited minority regime should possess some moral standards! You have used this public platform to attack an organization that has sacrificed everything for human dignity. If a man in your position cannot act with integrity in negotiations, how can the people of South Africa trust you? We do not seek petty concessions; we demand complete, non-racial democracy based on one person, one vote!"

The electrifying rebuke silenced the room. De Klerk realized that Mandela would never accept half-measures. Mandela's unyielding firmness preserved the integrity of the peace process, leading directly to the historic 1994 non-racial elections.
